titel: Schufa: The Secret Score That Rules Germany | Documentary
beschreibung:
A private company owned largely by banks holds data on around 68 million people in Germany, and for decades its score formula was a trade secret. Then Europe's highest court stepped in, and journalists reported a hidden archive of old data. Who checks the people who check you?

abschnitte.text: Imagine you have finally found the apartment. The rent is fair, the landlord likes you. Then he asks for one more piece of paper. A letter from a private company you never signed a contract with. And on that letter is a number that decides whether you get the keys.

In Germany, that company is called Schufa. It holds data on around sixty eight million people, almost every adult in the country. Banks, phone companies, online shops and landlords rely on it. And for decades, the way it calculated its scores was treated as a trade secret.

Then Europe's highest court stepped in. Then journalists reported a hidden archive of old data that, they say, should have been deleted long ago. And just one week ago, the rules changed again. So who really decides whether you can be trusted? And who checks the people who do the checking?

To understand Schufa, we have to go back to Berlin in nineteen twenty seven. The city's electricity company, Bewag, was selling household appliances on instalment plans. Irons, stoves, vacuum cleaners. The idea was simple. People who paid their electricity bill on time could probably be trusted to pay off a new stove as well.

suche: vintage black and white city street 1920s

bilder.unter: an idea from the power company

abschnitte.text: So a shared register was set up, recording who paid and who did not. Its name was a mouthful. Schutzgemeinschaft für allgemeine Kreditsicherung. Roughly, the protective association for general credit security. In short, Schufa. According to the city of Wiesbaden's official history, it had around one and a half million index cards just two years after it started.

After the Second World War, regional Schufa companies spread across West Germany. A national umbrella association was formed in nineteen fifty two and moved to Wiesbaden in nineteen fifty seven. In the year two thousand, the regional companies merged into Schufa Holding, which is still based in Wiesbaden today.

Think of Equifax or Experian. Schufa is not a government agency. It is a private company. And its owners are largely the very industry that uses its data. Savings banks, cooperative banks, private banks, and retailers.

Schufa says it holds around one billion data records on roughly sixty eight million people and six million companies. The information comes mainly from about ten thousand contract partners, plus public sources such as court registers of debtors and insolvency notices.

What is in there? Bank accounts, credit cards, loans, leasing contracts, and whether payments arrived on time. Schufa stresses that more than ninety percent of the people in its database have only positive entries. But positive entries are still data. Every account, every contract, every credit enquiry feeds the machine.

For most of its history, the heart of Schufa was a single number. A score, shown as a percentage, that was meant to predict how likely you are to pay. How exactly was it calculated? That, Schufa said, was a trade secret.

In January twenty fourteen, Germany's Federal Court of Justice agreed. A consumer from Hesse had sued to learn how their score was built. The court ruled that Schufa must tell people which of their data it stores and uses, but not the formula itself, and not how the criteria are weighted.

bilder.unter: formula stays secret, says Germany's top court

abschnitte.text: In twenty eighteen, two civil society groups tried something unusual. The Open Knowledge Foundation Germany and AlgorithmWatch asked ordinary people to request their own Schufa data and donate it. The project was called OpenSchufa. Its crowdfunding raised around forty three thousand euros, roughly fifty thousand dollars.

In November twenty eighteen, the news magazine Der Spiegel and the Bavarian public broadcaster BR published their analysis of around two thousand donated reports. One finding stood out. Schufa was running several versions of its score at the same time. Depending on which version a company requested, the same person could look more or less risky.

The journalists also concluded that the system could put some groups at a disadvantage. But they admitted the sample was voluntary and not representative, and would not stand up in court. Germany's justice minister at the time, Katarina Barley, demanded more transparency from credit agencies.
But the black box stayed closed. And people kept running into it in ordinary life. A rejected phone contract. A loan with a worse interest rate. An apartment that went to someone else.

Here is something many people do not know. Under European data protection law, the GDPR, everyone has the right to a free copy of the data a company holds about them. Schufa also sells a paid credit report, the kind many landlords like to see.

In February twenty twenty four, the privacy group noyb, founded by the Austrian activist Max Schrems, filed a complaint with the data protection authority in Hesse, the German state where Schufa is based. Its accusation was blunt. Schufa, it said, used manipulative design to hide the free option and push people towards the paid product.

noyb's headline: German credit agency earns millions through unlawful customer manipulation. Schufa rejected this. It said its free data copy went further than the law requires. noyb's own case page lists Schufa's response and noyb's reply, but no decision by the authority.

The business is valuable enough that investors wanted in. In twenty twenty one and twenty twenty two, the Swedish private equity firm EQT tried to take control of Schufa. Germany's competition authority cleared the plans in February twenty twenty two.

bilder.unter: a private equity bid for Schufa

abschnitte.text: But the savings banks and cooperative banks pushed back. According to Handelsblatt and Reuters, EQT eventually broke off talks. Schufa stayed in the hands of the banking industry. Which raises a question worth asking. If the companies that judge you are owned by the companies that lend to you, whose interests does the score serve first?

bilder.unter: judged by the lenders' own company

abschnitte.text: The real blow came from Luxembourg, home of the Court of Justice of the European Union. A consumer in Germany had been refused a loan after a negative Schufa score. They asked Schufa for an explanation and got only general information. The data protection authority in Hesse declined to act.

The consumer sued, and the Administrative Court of Wiesbaden sent the case to Luxembourg. On the seventh of December twenty twenty three, the judges ruled. Schufa had always argued that it only delivers a number, and the bank makes the decision.

bilder.unter: Court of Justice of the EU

abschnitte.text: The court disagreed. If a lender relies heavily on the score when deciding whether to grant credit, then calculating that score is itself an automated decision about a human being. And under the GDPR, such decisions are prohibited in principle, with narrow exceptions.

On the same day, the court decided two more cases, about people who had gone through personal bankruptcy. In Germany, when remaining debts are finally written off, that fact appears in an official public register for six months. Schufa, following an industry code of conduct, kept it for three years.
The court said that was not compatible with the GDPR. The whole point of a debt discharge is to let people return to economic life. Schufa shortened the period to six months.

In February twenty twenty five, the same court went further in an Austrian case against the credit agency Dun and Bradstreet. People affected by an automated score have a right to a real explanation. Not simply the algorithm, but an understandable account of which of their data was used, and how.

Trade secrets are no automatic excuse. A court or regulator must weigh them. Back in Wiesbaden, the administrative court applied these rulings in late twenty twenty five. Schufa, it found, must give people precise and comprehensible information about how their individual score is calculated. That ruling was not final.

Schufa was under pressure. In October twenty twenty three, after years of complaints from consumer advocates, it began deleting stored data about mobile phone contracts, so called positive data. According to reports, around twenty million customers were affected.

But the legal fight over that data continued. In October twenty twenty five, the Federal Court of Justice ruled that phone companies may in principle pass such contract data to Schufa to prevent fraud. What Schufa may do with it, including whether it can be used for credit scores, the court left open.

In December twenty twenty five, the same court ruled that keeping settled payment problems for up to three years is not automatically unlawful. Each case has to be weighed individually. Since twenty twenty five, a single payment problem that is paid within one hundred days can, under conditions, disappear after eighteen months instead.

Then, on the seventeenth of March twenty twenty six, Schufa launched what it called the world's first completely transparent credit score. The old percentage was replaced by a points scale from one hundred to nine hundred and ninety nine. Instead of roughly two hundred and fifty data attributes, it uses twelve published criteria. Payment problems are by far the strongest factor. And consumers got a free digital account to see their data and score at any time.

But there were catches. At launch, only about a quarter of Schufa's business partners used the new score. Companies may keep using the old one until the end of twenty twenty eight. And critics called the reform, above all, a marketing success for Schufa. Transparency, but on Schufa's own terms?

Then came July twenty twenty six. A joint investigation by the public broadcaster NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that Schufa keeps a separate archive of historical data on around sixty eight million people.

According to the reporting, it includes old loans, card debts, wage garnishments, private insolvencies, and debts that were paid off years ago. Data that, in the view of the journalists and the legal experts they quoted, Schufa should have deleted long ago. And when people requested their free data copy, this archive reportedly did not show up.

What was it for? According to the reports, Schufa uses the archive to test its models, by calculating what score a person would have received at an earlier point in time. Test results were reportedly passed on to business partners. Some customers could also retrieve historical scores.

Schufa confirmed that it holds historical data. But it rejects the term shadow database. It says the data is used only for purposes such as testing, quality control, model development and legal defence, that it does not affect anyone's current score, and that this storage is lawful.

Critics see it very differently. In August twenty twenty six, noyb sent Schufa a formal cease and desist letter, demanding that it stop keeping data beyond the official deletion periods. In September, Schufa refused. It said it would defend its position in court, if necessary all the way to the Federal Court of Justice.

noyb has announced a lawsuit and is collecting names for a possible class action for damages. According to media reports, it considers around five hundred euros per person conceivable, a little under six hundred dollars. When we made this video, we found no report that a lawsuit had been filed, and no court had ruled. Schufa maintains it acted lawfully.

Think about it. A person pays off a debt, waits for years, and the entry finally disappears from their file. Officially. But according to the reporting, a copy of their past may still exist somewhere. Is that quality control? Or is it a second memory nobody agreed to?

Last month, on the twenty first of October twenty twenty six, the Federal Court of Justice ruled in four parallel cases. Scoring can count as a decision under data protection law. But Schufa only has to explain a score in detail if a contract really depended on it.

bilder.unter: four rulings, Federal Court of Justice

abschnitte.text: There is help for consumers, though. Anyone who can show that a score was sent to a company, and that a loan was refused shortly afterwards, benefits from a presumption in their favour. The cases were sent back to a lower court, so the final word is still open.

And since the twentieth of November twenty twenty six, exactly one week ago, a new German law applies. Section thirty seven a of the Federal Data Protection Act, passed together with the new European rules on consumer credit. According to legal analyses, it bans certain data from certain scores. Address data, account transactions, data from social networks, and sensitive personal data. And people can ask how the criteria are weighted.

So what does this mean for you? If you live in Germany, request your free data copy at least once a year. Check it for errors. If you are refused a loan or a contract, ask whether a score was decisive, and ask for an explanation. You are entitled to one.

And if you live elsewhere, credit scores decide who gets loans and apartments in your country too. The European rulings make one thing very clear. Being scored by a machine is not a neutral act. It is a decision about you.

Schufa began almost a century ago with index cards and a simple idea. People who pay their electricity bill will probably pay for their stove. Today, it holds something like the financial memory of a nation.

And nearly every step towards transparency in recent years came from outside. Citizens who donated their data. Journalists who kept digging. A privacy activist from Austria. Judges in Luxembourg and in Karlsruhe. Schufa presents itself as a pioneer of transparency. Its critics say it only moved when it had to.

So here is the question. Should a private company, owned largely by banks, hold the financial memory of an entire country? Or would you trust the state with it even less? Tell me in the comments. And if you want more stories about who really holds power over your money, subscribe.
